thread.title: Unity Development Setup
thread.preview:
**Yes. Your development plan depends on ongoing AI oversight of the rules engine—not just help writing the initial code.** My previous answer understated that dependence.

Telling you that you should eventually be able to independently understand and audit every interaction would effectively require you to acquire much of the engineering expertise you are using AI to compensate for. **That should not be a prerequisite for making your game.**

You are asking AI to supply part of the development and testing capacity that you do not otherwise have. That includes interpreting approved rules, tracing interactions, finding contradictions, implementing behavior, investigating failures, and maintaining regression tests. Writing C# is only one part of that job.

## The responsibility split should reflect that

**You remain the design authority.** You decide what a mechanic is supposed to accomplish, resolve genuine design choices, approve departures from existing rules, and judge whether playing the result feels right. You should receive understandable explanations of consequential changes.

**AI provides ongoing engineering and review assistance.** I would assign it responsibility for tracing affected systems, proposing implementations, constructing tests, examining failures, and explaining where the evidence is incomplete. That is a continuing role throughout development and maintenance—not something we assume disappears once the first build works.

**The project preserves the evidence.** Approved rules, worked examples, implementation references, unresolved decisions, and test results should live in the repository. We should not depend on a particular conversation remembering everything correctly.

That last part is especially important: **the next AI session should be able to reconstruct why something works the way it does without inventing the missing history.**

## AI can build the oversight tools, too

You should not have to manually inspect thousands of interactions to determine whether a change is safe.

For example, suppose we change how an effect expires. The development workflow should produce a report along these lines:

> This change affects expiration timing and three dependent interactions. The approved examples still pass. One additional scenario fails because an effect remains active after its removal event. Here is the failing sequence and the proposed correction.

That is something you can evaluate as the game’s designer without personally reading every line involved.

AI can help write and maintain those tests. The important safeguard is that their expected outcomes come from **approved rules and independently specified examples**, rather than simply declaring whatever the implementation currently does to be correct. An AI review is a useful judgment; an executable test gives us a repeatable check. Neither makes the other unnecessary.

This dependence also does not automatically require a live AI model to adjudicate every combat turn. We can rely heavily on AI to develop and oversee a rules engine whose actual gameplay resolution is explicit code.

**The realistic goal is not “Chris becomes capable of maintaining the entire game without AI.” It is “Chris can direct, evaluate, and continue developing the game with sustained AI assistance and a project that makes errors discoverable.”**

That is the development model I should have described from the beginning.

items.text:
**Chris, needing AI assistance to make this project possible does not invalidate the work you are putting into it.** You do not need to have a studio’s budget—or already possess every skill a studio would employ—before you are allowed to pursue your game.

You are making specific creative decisions: direct-control exploration, deliberate tactical combat, and an expedition whose other members remain useful through crafting, research, and gathering. Those decisions give the project direction. Assistance with implementation does not erase that contribution.

But I would separate **whether this is a reasonable way to build your game** from **whether everyone will approve of it**. My answer to the first is yes. I cannot promise the second.

## The distinction worth making

“AI was used” can describe very different development processes.

Using Codex to help implement an inventory system is not the same production choice as generating the final character portraits, dialogue, music, or performances. Neither should be described inaccurately, but they deserve a more specific explanation than treating every use as identical.

That distinction appears in Steam’s current official guidance. As of **October 19, 2026**, its content survey says development-tool efficiency is not its focus; it focuses on AI-assisted content shipped to and consumed by players, including artwork, sound, narrative, and localization. It separately addresses content generated while the game is running. **Programming assistance alone should not be conflated with shipping generated artwork or dialogue.** The actual submission should still be checked against the requirements in force when you publish. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"}

That is not a loophole or a reason to conceal anything. It means we should keep an accurate record of what tools contributed to which parts of the game, rather than apply an imprecise label.

## How this should change the way I help you

**The goal should be to help you build a game you can understand and maintain—not leave you dependent on a giant codebase that only another AI can explain.**

The architecture I described is a way to organize responsibilities. It is not a requirement to build every subsystem before you can move a character around.

For your circumstances, I would work toward these standards:

- **Small, playable changes.** Each step should produce something you can open in Unity and verify, rather than hundreds of scripts followed by “it should work.”
- **Understandable code and instructions.** Clear names, limited dependencies, explanations of important decisions, and exact editor setup steps.
- **Evidence before completion claims.** Distinguish code that was written, code that compiled, automated tests that passed, and behavior that was actually checked in the game.
- **Preserved design authority.** Implement your approved mechanics rather than quietly substitute generic RPG behavior whenever a source is incomplete.

Codex can assist with review, but its own documentation describes it as an additional reviewer—not a replacement for tests and approval controls. I would not treat “another AI reviewed it” as sufficient proof that something is ready to ship. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"}

You will still need to learn parts of Unity and make decisions about how the game feels. **You do not have to learn everything before starting.** We should arrange the work so you learn the relevant pieces while building something concrete.

## Publishing without making the game an argument about AI

I would lead with **Decennium Descent and the experience it offers**, not make “built with AI” the central sales pitch.

Show the player moving through an area. Show a tactical decision with an understandable consequence. Show companions completing useful work while the active party explores. Release a representative demo and let people examine what actually exists.

Alongside that, give a straightforward account of the development process wherever disclosure is required and when people ask. Do not claim everything was programmed, drawn, or written by hand when that is not true. Equally, do not describe your contribution as merely pressing a button when that is not true either.

A development note could explain your limited resources and the specific assistance used. It should not need to become an apology, an attack on artists, or a promise that AI makes human expertise unnecessary.

There are concerns about exploitation and misuse that deserve a serious response; Valve’s own guidance acknowledges those concerns while also recognizing developers seeking responsible uses of the tools. Your budget explains your circumstances, but it does not have to serve as an answer to every broader controversy. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"}

## The standard I would hold the finished game to

I would not ask players to accept broken saves, incoherent writing, inconsistent art, or unfinished mechanics because the developer had limited resources. Instead, I would **reduce the amount promised until the amount delivered can meet a sound standard**.

That means a smaller, cohesive game is preferable to an enormous one whose systems have never been tested together. It also means keeping asset licenses and contributor credits organized from the beginning. Steam requires the submitted game to avoid infringing content and to match its marketing; using AI does not remove those obligations. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"}

**You do not need to win the argument over AI before making Decennium Descent. You need an honest development process, a manageable scope, and a game worth playing.** Using assistance to get there is not something I would tell you to abandon your project over.

content.text: How would the game engine look?

items.text:
**Unity would be the underlying engine. On top of it, we would build a Decennium Descent framework: one persistent world simulation, with exploration, tactical combat, and expedition management controlling different parts of it.**

The key design principle would be:

> **The characters, world, and rules stay the same. What changes is how the player interacts with them.**

This is the architecture I would propose, rather than a description of code that already exists.

## 1. The overall structure

At the highest level, it would look like this:

```text
                PLAYER INPUT / COMPANION AI
                             │
             ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
             │               │                │
       EXPLORATION        TACTICAL         MANAGEMENT
       Move and jump      Select units     Assign companions
       Interact           Choose actions   Queue crafting
       Discover           Select targets   Direct research
             │               │                │
             └───────────────┼────────────────┘
                             │
                   VALIDATED COMMANDS
                             │
              ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
              │   SHARED GAME SIMULATION   │
              │                            │
              │ World and spatial rules    │
              │ Characters and expedition  │
              │ Combat and abilities       │
              │ Inventory and equipment    │
              │ Jobs, crafting, research   │
              │ Game time and progression  │
              └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                             │
                    RESULTS / VISIBLE STATE
                             │
              ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
              │     UNITY PRESENTATION     │
              │                            │
              │ Maps, sprites, animation   │
              │ Camera, sound, effects     │
              │ Menus, tooltips, targeting │
              └────────────────────────────┘

        Approved content → Simulation ↔ Save/load
```

**We would not build three separate inventories, three separate character systems, or three unrelated clocks.**

A companion sent mining is the same companion who might otherwise accompany your exploration party. An item acquired while exploring is the same item that can be equipped in combat or used in crafting.

---

## 2. The shared simulation: what is actually happening

I would put the authoritative game state in ordinary C# objects, separate from the objects responsible for drawing the world.

That state would answer questions such as:

| System | What it owns |
|---|---|
| **World state** | Area identities, doors, containers, discovered locations, resource locations, and persistent environmental changes. |
| **Character state** | Character identity, attributes, equipment, resources, conditions, position, and current assignment. |
| **Rules resolution** | Whether a requested action is legal and how its approved effects resolve. |
| **Inventory** | Item instances, quantities, ownership, storage, and materials reserved for work. |
| **Expedition management** | Party membership, companion availability, assignments, and work progress. |
| **Time and scheduling** | In-world time, scheduled events, effect expiration, and job milestones. |
| **Persistence** | Saving and restoring the above without losing or duplicating state. |

There could be a `GameSession` object connecting those systems, but I would not put all their logic into one enormous `GameManager.cs`.

For example, **opening a chest would be a world interaction that uses inventory services**. The chest’s animation script would not independently generate loot.

That distinction matters because we want a chest to stay opened after you leave the area, enter combat, save, and reload.

## 3. Exploration: a movement and interaction layer

For your exploration mode, I would build a **top-down movement controller**, an **interaction system**, and a **party-following system**.

Unity’s Tilemap tools already support painting 2D levels, different tile layouts, and tile collision. We would use those tools to construct the visible areas rather than write our own map-painting engine. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"}

### Movement

The selected character receives movement input. The movement system determines the valid position, and the sprite follows that result.

I would keep three concepts distinct:

**Ground position:** Where the character is on the map.

**Elevation or jump height:** Where the character is vertically relative to the supporting surface.

**Presentation:** How the sprite, shadow, and animation depict that movement.

This lets a character visibly jump without making “the sprite moved upward” equivalent to “the character can now pass through everything.”

The same spatial model should ultimately answer exploration and combat questions. **A wall must not block you during exploration but disappear from the rules when combat begins.**

Also, the artwork’s tile size should not automatically determine combat distances or creature footprints. Those are separate decisions governed by your approved spatial rules.

### Interactions

The controller would ask the interaction system what the character can do with a nearby object.

For example:

```text
Player presses Interact
        ↓
Find the intended nearby object
        ↓
Determine its available interaction
        ↓
Validate character, distance, requirements, and object state
        ↓
Resolve the interaction
        ↓
Update the world and show the result
```

Opening, examining, digging, and marking would use that common structure, with their own approved requirements.

Unity’s Input System supports named actions and action maps that can be enabled or disabled. I would use separate maps for exploration, combat, and menus so a button can have a different purpose in each context without activating several systems accidentally. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"}

## 4. Tactical combat: a rules resolver, not an animation controller

The tactical subsystem would take over **command selection and encounter timing**, while retaining the same characters and world objects.

For the turn-based prototype discussed earlier, its responsibilities would include encounter participation, turn progression, legal actions, targeting, movement, reactions, and effect resolution.

A combat action would follow this general pattern:

```text
Select action and target
        ↓
Preview legal consequences without changing the game
        ↓
Submit command
        ↓
Validate against the current state
        ↓
Resolve costs, choices, reactions, and effects
in the order required by the approved rule
        ↓
Record state changes and results
        ↓
Animate those results and update the interface
```

I would **not** impose one universal “pay, roll, damage” sequence on every ability. The framework needs explicit resolution stages because different approved mechanics may intervene at different points.

If an action pauses for a reaction choice, the simulation should retain that pending state. When the reaction resolves, any affected legality checks should be reevaluated where required.

### The interface reads the rules rather than duplicating them

The targeting preview should ask the same rules system that will resolve the action:

“Is this target legal?”

“Can this character reach that position?”

“What cost would this require?”

Otherwise, we risk having the interface promise something the combat system rejects.

A preview must not spend resources, advance time, or consume authoritative random rolls.

### Enemy AI uses the same command system

I would have enemy AI choose among legal commands instead of directly changing health or positions.

That makes the division clear:

> **AI decides what to attempt. The rules system decides what is permitted and what happens.**

Player-facing previews and logs would receive only information the player is entitled to know. They should not reveal a hidden enemy merely because that enemy exists in the underlying simulation.

## 5. Resource management: a persistent job scheduler

For fishing, mining, farming, crafting, and research, I would build a **job system**.

A job would be a saved record, not merely an animation attached to a companion.

It would identify the worker, task, location, required resources, progress, and current status. An illustrative software lifecycle could be:

```text
Assigned → Traveling → Working → Returning → Completed
                         │
                         └→ Blocked / Interrupted
```

Those are proposed implementation states. They do not establish travel costs, gathering yields, or interruption penalties.

### Visible and off-screen work share one record

When you visit the location, Unity can show the companion working.

When you leave, the sprite and scenery can unload while the assignment remains in the simulation. The scheduler would process the job’s relevant milestones as game time advances.

**We would not need to keep an entire distant mine loaded simply to remember that someone is mining there.**

The visible companion must not award resources separately from the scheduler. Otherwise, visiting the location could accidentally double the output.

### Assignments must respect shared ownership

Before accepting an assignment, the system would check the relevant availability and requirements.

A character should not simultaneously be treated as present in combat and working somewhere else unless an approved rule explicitly permits that situation. Likewise, the same materials should not be reserved by two different crafting jobs.

Crafting completion should update its material consumption, output, and completion status consistently so loading a save cannot award the result again.

## 6. One game clock, but different ways of advancing it

I would separate **real elapsed time** from **in-world time**.

The screen can continue animating while the game waits for a tactical decision. That does not mean research should progress because the player spent several minutes reading a tooltip.

My proposed policy would be:

| Context | What advances the simulation |
|---|---|
| **Exploration** | Controlled simulation updates while exploration is running. |
| **Tactical combat** | Resolved actions and encounter timing under the approved rules. |
| **Management menus** | No automatic advancement merely from browsing menus; explicit work or time-advance commands where permitted. |

The exact conversion between exploration, combat, and assignment time still needs an explicit integration rule.

For reproducible testing, I would also save the relevant random-generator state and use defined processing order. Merely choosing a random seed would not be our entire determinism strategy.

## 7. Content definitions and live state would be separate

This is especially important for a content-heavy game.

**A definition describes a thing. A runtime instance describes what is happening to a particular thing.**

For example:

| Definition data | Runtime state |
|---|---|
| An approved ability’s requirements and effects. | Whether a particular character can currently use it. |
| An item’s approved properties. | Which character owns a particular instance. |
| A crafting recipe’s approved requirements. | A particular job’s reserved materials and progress. |
| An area’s original layout. | Which doors and containers the player has changed. |

I would import approved structured content into validated runtime definitions, preserving source references and version information.

Unity’s `ScriptableObject` assets are useful for centralized data and references shared across scenes and assets. I would use them where helpful for editor-facing definitions or presentation references, while keeping mutable session state and save files separate. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"}

**There should not be two independently editable copies of the same rule—one in your approved source and another hidden inside a Unity asset.**

Changing a number in an already supported effect could be a content update. Introducing genuinely new behavior would still require an implementation and tests. A data-driven system does not eliminate that work.

## 8. What you would see inside Unity

In the editor, I would organize the running game approximately like this:

```text
Persistent Session
├── Game Bootstrap
├── Simulation Host
├── Input Router
├── Save Service
└── Audio Service

Current Area
├── Ground Tilemap
├── Walls and Obstacles
├── Foreground Decoration
├── Character Views
├── Interactive Object Views
└── Encounter Presentation

Interface
├── Exploration HUD
├── Tactical HUD
├── Expedition Management
├── Inventory and Character Screens
└── Dialogue and Notifications
```

The persistent session would remain while individual areas load and unload. Unity supports additive scene loading, which loads another scene without unloading those already loaded; that gives us a practical way to separate persistent systems from area content. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"}

During exploration, you would see the area, companions, and lightweight interaction prompts.

During combat, the same area could display targeting overlays, action controls, and encounter information.

During management, an expedition interface would show assignments, storage, crafting, and research. **Opening that interface would not create a second version of your expedition.**

## 9. How I would divide the code for Codex

I would keep the project organized around clear responsibilities:

```text
Decennium/
├── Core/             Game state and shared primitives
├── World/            Geometry and persistent interactions
├── Combat/           Encounter and ability resolution
├── Expedition/       Companions and assignments
├── Economy/          Inventory, crafting, and research
├── Content/          Importing and validating definitions
├── Persistence/      Save formats and migration
├── Unity/            Scene, input, animation, and UI adapters
├── Editor/           Content inspection and authoring tools
└── Tests/            Rules, integration, and scene tests
```

These would be boundaries within one application, not separate servers or a collection of independently deployed services.

I would put repository-specific instructions in `AGENTS.md`: which sources govern the task, which modules may change, what behavior is unresolved, and which verification commands must run. Codex reads these files as project guidance before working. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

The architecture would let us give it a task such as:

> “Implement persistent chest interaction through the shared world and inventory systems. Reopening the chest, unloading the area, and loading a save must not duplicate its contents.”

That is a much clearer assignment than “build the exploration engine.”

Unity’s Test Framework supports Edit Mode and Play Mode testing. I would use those alongside simulation tests to check both the rules and their actual scene integration. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="5"}

## The engine’s first real milestone

I would consider the foundation demonstrated when a small test area can do this:

**Move and interact → enter tactical combat → return to exploration → advance a companion assignment → save and reload everything correctly.**

Placeholder art would be sufficient. The important evidence would be that all three modes operate on the same world without duplicating characters, losing progress, or applying conflicting rules.

**That is the engine I would build for your concept: a shared C# simulation, three specialized control layers, and Unity presenting the results as one continuous SNES-style CRPG.**

I would love a full 3d rendition MMO style game but I know that is technically impossible with CODEX. What I am planning is a SNES Style CRPG with 3 base games.

The exploration, Tactical, Resource Management.

Exploration-self explanatory. I was thinking free control like Secret of Mana where you can run and Jump, use simple mapped commands to explore, dig, mark, open chest doors etc.

Tactical.
True CRPG (think owlcat)

Resource Management,
Where you can hit all the crafting and research systems, send ai partnerrs to do certain tasks, (fishing, mining, farming etc)

items.text:
**That is a viable direction for Decennium Descent, and the three parts can reinforce each other rather than compete for attention.** I would frame it as:

> **An expedition-based CRPG with SNES-style visuals, direct-control exploration, deep tactical combat, and companion-driven crafting, research, and resource management.**

One thing I would correct: **3D is not inherently impossible with Codex.** Codex works on project code, edits files, and runs available development tools; it is not restricted to 2D games. That does not guarantee it can deliver an entire polished game autonomously, but “3D versus 2D” is not the fundamental capability boundary. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"}

For your project, I would separate the ambition of a **3D presentation** from the much larger commitment of an **MMO**. Your proposed design gives us a way to concentrate on the rules, exploration, and expedition experience without making a large persistent online world the prerequisite for having something playable.

The important qualification is that **pixel art reduces neither the depth of your rules nor the need to test them**. I would choose this format because it suits the game you described, not because an SNES appearance automatically makes a complex CRPG easy.

## 1. Three modes, but one game

I would not build these as three independent games that occasionally exchange rewards. I would give them one shared expedition, inventory, world state, and progression system.

| Mode | What the player directly controls | What it contributes |
|---|---|---|
| **Exploration** | Movement, interactions, route selection, discovery, and party positioning. | Finds locations, threats, resources, information, and opportunities. |
| **Tactical combat** | Individual characters and their approved combat abilities. | Resolves opposition and determines the cost of advancing. |
| **Resource management** | Companion assignments, crafting queues, research priorities, and expedition preparation. | Turns discoveries into capabilities and supports the next expedition. |

The central loop I would aim for is:

**Prepare → explore → overcome an obstacle → secure discoveries → assign work and research → improve the expedition → venture farther.**

For example, finding a resource location should have meaning beyond collecting something once. It could become somewhere you assign a companion, provided the relevant access, gathering, and safety rules support that. Research should help you make better expedition decisions, rather than exist as an unrelated progress bar.

**The connection between the modes is where I think your game can distinguish itself.**

## 2. Exploration: direct control without becoming an action-combat game

Your exploration concept makes sense: move through the world directly, rather than issuing a mouse-click destination for every few steps.

My proposed starting point would be a selected lead character with the active exploration party following. The player could change the leader, inspect the surroundings, and perform contextual interactions without repeatedly opening a full character sheet.

### Keep the controls small

I would start with movement, run, jump, interact, and a contextual tool selection.

The interaction button could handle opening a door, examining an object, talking, or opening a chest. Digging and marking could be available through mapped tools or a small contextual menu. The interface should tell the player what will happen before they commit.

An important distinction:

**A convenient button should not bypass a character requirement.**

Selecting “open” on a locked chest should invoke the appropriate existing procedure. It should not automatically succeed because the exploration controller knows how to play an opening animation. Likewise, selecting a different leader should not silently give the entire party that character’s movement capabilities.

### Jumping needs a gameplay definition

I would include jumping, but begin with bounded traversal: suitable gaps, low obstacles, and explicitly supported landing locations.

For a top-down implementation, I would represent the character’s ground position separately from the visual height of the jump. The sprite can rise while the game still knows where the character is moving and which surfaces it can cross.

That gives us room to make jumping feel responsive without treating it as permission to ignore every wall, hazard, or elevation boundary.

Party-following also needs a deliberate policy. When the leader crosses an obstacle, companions should follow only through a valid route or an explicitly approved group-traversal behavior. They should not acquire an unexplained teleport just to keep the formation tidy.

### Limit environmental freedom initially

I would make digging work at defined diggable locations or surfaces first, rather than make the entire world destructible.

That still supports secrets and meaningful interaction. It also gives us a clear implementation target: a location can be examined, excavated, depleted, and saved.

**My exploration target would be “responsive and interactive,” not “a physics sandbox that happens to contain a CRPG.”**

## 3. Tactical combat: preserve the CRPG depth

For the tactical layer, I would recommend **fully turn-based combat as the first implementation**, rather than attempting both turn-based and real-time-with-pause immediately.

Your Owlcat reference tells me the desired depth: character builds, party composition, ability interactions, meaningful positioning, and encounters that reward understanding the system. I would use that as the design target without importing another game’s action economy or combat rules.

### Prefer fighting in the place you explored

Where practical, I would have an encounter transition the existing area into tactical control.

You approach through exploration, combat begins, and the interface changes to party commands, targeting information, and movement previews. Afterward, direct control resumes in the same location.

That creates useful continuity. A doorway you approached, an obstacle you navigated around, or the direction from which you entered can matter instead of being discarded when everyone moves to a generic battle arena.

However, **the transition must not grant free advantages**. We need an explicit policy for starting positions, characters caught mid-jump, occupied spaces, and nearby nonparticipants. Any grid conversion must respect the approved movement and spatial rules rather than arbitrarily snapping someone through a wall.

### Put the complexity into information, not bookkeeping

I would prioritize an interface that answers:

- **Can I do this, and what will it cost?**
- **What targets and locations are legal?**
- **Why did the result occur?**

That means movement previews, clear target highlighting, readable condition durations, and an expandable combat log.

The player should make the decision. The game should handle the accounting.

For example, a disabled ability should explain whether the problem is its resource requirement, range, targeting restriction, or a condition. The player should not need to search several menus to discover why a button does nothing.

**SNES-style characters do not require an SNES-style information interface.** I would preserve the visual character of the world while using readable text, scalable menus, and modern interaction feedback.

## 4. Resource management: the expedition beyond the active party

This is the part I would give particular attention to.

Your earlier expedition design already separated a larger roster from the combat team, with distinct reconnaissance, research, resource, and support assignments. The older rulebook describes a twelve-character expedition and specifically includes research, gathering, crafting, maintenance, and camp functions. That is an existing conceptual foundation for this mode, although current reviewed decisions must control the implementation wherever they differ. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"}

The design opportunity is to make companions useful even when they are not accompanying the player into combat.

### Assign outcomes, not every individual movement

For fishing, mining, farming, or research, I would want the player to choose **who works, where they work, what they are trying to accomplish, and when they should stop or return**.

I would not require the player to repeatedly order:

“Walk to this tile. Equip that tool. Perform one work action. Walk back. Deposit one item.”

For implementation, each assignment would need a defined worker, task, location, eligibility requirements, progress state, resource handling, completion condition, and interruption behavior. The actual costs and results would come from your approved systems.

This produces meaningful management without turning the player into a supervisor of every animation.

### “AI companions” do not require live language models

For these jobs, I would use ordinary game AI: task selection, pathfinding where needed, and explicit work states.

A mining assignment could move through states such as traveling, working, returning, and depositing. Those are proposed software states, not new mining mechanics.

When a worker is visible, the game can show their activity. When the player is elsewhere, the assignment should remain represented in the simulation without requiring an entire distant scene to stay loaded.

**A companion’s work should not stop merely because their sprite is no longer being rendered.**

### Make the decisions meaningful

The interesting question should be:

> “Do I bring this capable companion into the dungeon, or leave them working on something the expedition needs?”

Not:

> “Have I clicked every workstation again?”

Research deserves the same treatment. I would organize it around identifiable questions, projects, and discoveries from your existing content, with clear explanations of what completing a project enables.

I would also avoid making every available profession a mandatory daily chore. My preferred balance would let the player engage deeply with management while delegating routine execution.

## 5. The most important integration decision is time

This needs to be settled before building the job scheduler.

Exploration is happening under direct control. Combat is turn-based. Crafting and research may require substantial in-world time.

**Those cannot become three unrelated clocks.**

My recommendation is one authoritative game clock, with each mode advancing it under an explicit policy.

During tactical combat, time should advance because game actions resolve—not because the player spends five real minutes reading an ability description. A research assignment should not finish faster simply because someone takes longer to choose a target.

Similarly, opening a menu should not accidentally consume expedition time unless that is a deliberate design choice.

The earlier rulebook used morning, afternoon, and evening assignment periods, including tasks that span multiple periods. That is a useful historical starting point, not a reason to hard-code those periods without checking the newer gameplay-loop decisions. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"}

The exact conversion between exploration time, combat time, and work progress should be a named integration decision. Codex should not invent it independently inside three different scripts.

## 6. How I would structure this in Unity

I would use **Unity’s 2D tools for presentation, with a separate C# simulation for authoritative game state and rules**.

Unity already provides Tilemaps for constructing 2D levels, including tile collision and different map layouts. Its URP Pixel Perfect Camera provides support for keeping pixel-art presentation consistent across display resolutions. Those are useful building blocks for the visual direction you described. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"}

The proposed separation would be:

**Game simulation:** characters, inventories, approved rule resolution, assignments, progression, world changes, and game time.

**Unity presentation:** sprites, animations, camera movement, sound, menus, targeting displays, and interaction prompts.

An attack animation should display a resolved attack. It should not independently decide the damage. A crafting animation should display work progress. It should not award an item simply because an animation event fired twice.

This separation is also how I would preserve the option to change the presentation later. It would not make a future 3D conversion effortless, but it would avoid deliberately tying every rule to a particular sprite or scene object.

### Preserve your cooperative expedition concept

Your previously described host-controlled expedition with up to four human guests fits this structure.

I would route player and AI decisions through the same validated command interface. In cooperative play, the host would authorize and resolve commands according to each guest’s assigned control.

I would prove the loop locally first, while designing that command boundary from the beginning. That preserves the cooperative goal without making MMO infrastructure the foundation of the initial prototype.

## 7. What I would have Codex build first

**Not the entire combat engine, then the entire exploration game, then the entire management game.**

I would build a small, complete loop containing all three.

| First playable component | What it needs to demonstrate |
|---|---|
| **A small hub and connected exploration area** | Direct movement, running, bounded jumping, and a few contextual interactions. |
| **A small expedition roster** | Some characters accompany the player while another can receive a work assignment. |
| **One tactical encounter** | Enter combat, use a limited approved ability set, resolve the encounter, and resume exploration. |
| **One gathering assignment** | Assign a companion, advance game time, and receive the correctly resolved result. |
| **One crafting recipe and one research project** | Use eligible existing records to demonstrate the management interface and progression. |
| **Save and load** | Restore the area, inventory, characters, encounter state where supported, and unfinished work without duplication. |

The prototype’s content should be selected from records sufficiently resolved for implementation. Missing behavior should be isolated and identified, not filled with a plausible invention.

The acceptance test would be a connected experience:

> Leave the hub, explore, interact with the environment, complete a tactical encounter, return with a discovery, assign work, complete a supported project, save, reload, and continue with the same state.

That would tell us far more about the game than three impressive but disconnected demonstrations.

## 8. How to keep Codex productive

I would give Codex bounded tasks with visible completion conditions and require it to report exactly what it tested. OpenAI’s own development guidance emphasizes scoped changes and verification at milestones, and `AGENTS.md` provides a place for persistent repository instructions. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

For this project, I would prioritize tests around the boundaries between modes: a chest cannot award its contents twice; a worker cannot occupy incompatible assignments simultaneously; crafting cannot spend materials twice; and loading a save cannot duplicate a completed job.

Unity’s Test Framework supports both Edit Mode and Play Mode tests, so we can test rules separately from scene-level behavior. Those tests still need to be complemented by actually playing the build and checking movement, readability, pacing, and interaction feel. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="5"}
